vignette:
Sameer speaks of his shop as if it’s a part of his own body. He knows the worn patch on the linoleum by the drink cooler, the specific groan the stockroom door makes in humid weather. His parents had run this small grocery for thirty years before passing it to him, and for a long time, it was his greatest source of pride. Now, it often feels like a cage. Every chime of the bell above the door sends a jolt through his spine, and he has to consciously stop himself from scanning the street for a car that he knows will never be there again.

He met Rohan two years ago. At first, it was intoxicating. Rohan was charismatic, confident, and showered Sameer with an intensity of affection he’d never known. He loved that Sameer had his own business, calling him “the king of his castle.” They moved in together quickly. The early days were a blur of shared dreams, planning expansions for the shop, and feeling, for the first time, like he was truly building a life with someone.

The shift was subtle at first. It started with comments about the way Sameer handled the finances. “You’re too soft with the suppliers,” Rohan would say, his voice laced with a concern that felt like care. Then came the jealousy, quiet accusations about friendly customers that morphed into demands to see Sameer’s phone. The castle began to feel smaller, its walls closing in. Sameer started walking on eggshells, measuring his words, his smiles, his very presence, to keep the peace.

The first time Rohan pushed him, it was during an argument about inventory. Sameer stumbled back against a shelf of canned goods, the metallic clatter echoing in the sudden silence. The shock was colder than the fear. Rohan’s apology was immediate and desperate, full of tears and promises. Sameer, desperate to believe the man he loved was still in there, forgave him. It was a mistake that would be repeated, each cycle of rage and remorse escalating, until the night Rohan’s anger left him with a split lip and a dislocated shoulder. His brother had to come and get him, packing a bag for him while Sameer sat numbly on the sofa, unable to look at his own reflection in the dark television screen.

That was ten months ago. Now, there is Priya. She is gentle in a way that feels foreign, almost suspicious. Her touch is light, her voice is even, and her patience seems infinite. But Sameer is living in a different reality. When she comes up behind him while he’s making tea and rests a hand on his back, he flinches so violently he spills boiling water on the counter. The apology tumbles out of him, frantic and full of a shame so profound it chokes him. He sees the hurt flicker in her eyes before she masks it with understanding, and he hates himself for it.

Sleep offers no escape. He often wakes up thrashing, the phantom sensation of hands around his throat, his own muffled shouts caught in his chest. He’ll lie awake for hours afterward, staring at the ceiling, his body humming with an alert terror that has nowhere to go. During the day, he is a ghost in his own life. A customer will ask a question, and Sameer will realize he hasn’t heard a word, his mind caught in a silent, looping film of a past argument. He feels a constant, simmering anger just beneath his skin, and it erupts over meaningless things—a late delivery, a misplaced box of tea bags. He feels fundamentally broken, a fraud in this new, kind relationship. He looks at Priya, who sees a future for them, and all he can think is that she is in love with a man who no longer exists.
